facts.statement: This brain area is located in the back part of the frontal lobe and consists of several linked zones.
The main components are Brodmann area 4, known as the primary motor cortex, and area 6, which includes premotor and supplementary regions.
The primary role of this cortex is to organize, choose, and carry out movements that are under conscious control.
It converts intended actions into specific neural signals that travel down to the brainstem and spinal cord to control muscles.
This processing allows for precise and skilled movements of the eyes, facial muscles, and limbs.
Direct neural connections from this cortex to motor neurons are essential for the detailed control of finger movements.
The structure of this area influences the specific movement problems that occur following a stroke or degenerative conditions.
Understanding this region's layout is critical for planning brain surgeries and developing neural technologies.

en.text: Situated in the posterior frontal lobe, the motor cortex comprises linked zones, primarily Brodmann area 4 (the primary motor cortex) and area 6, which contains premotor and supplementary regions.
This structure organizes, selects, and executes consciously controlled movements by converting intended actions into specific neural signals that descend to the brainstem and spinal cord.
Such processing enables precise, skilled movements of the eyes, face, and limbs, while direct connections to motor neurons are essential for detailed finger control.

es.text: Situada en el lóbulo frontal posterior, la corteza motora está compuesta por zonas interconectadas, principalmente el área 4 de Brodmann (la corteza motora primaria) y el área 6, que alberga las regiones premotoras y suplementarias.

Esta estructura organiza, selecciona y ejecuta los movimientos controlados de forma consciente, transformando las acciones intencionadas en señales neuronales específicas que descienden hacia el tronco encefálico y la médula espinal.

Este procesamiento permite movimientos precisos y hábiles de los ojos, la cara y las extremidades, mientras que las conexiones directas con las neuronas motoras son esenciales para el control detallado de los dedos.

facts.statement: The hippocampus is a key structure found in the brains of people and numerous other vertebrate species.
In humans, this region works alongside the dentate gyrus and subiculum to form the hippocampal formation within the limbic system.
It helps transfer short-term memories into long-term storage and supports spatial memory needed for navigating the environment.
In primates, the structure sits in the archicortex, which is one of three allocortex areas, and exists in both brain hemispheres.
The region sends direct neural signals to the neocortex and receives indirect signals back from it.
In Alzheimer's and other dementias, this area is often among the first parts of the brain to suffer damage.
Early signs of such damage typically include losing short-term memories and feeling disoriented.
Severe injury to both sides of the structure can cause anterograde amnesia, which prevents the creation of new memories.
Long-term potentiation, a type of neural plasticity, was first identified in this brain region.
In rodents, specific neurons called place cells activate when the animal moves through a particular location in its surroundings.

problems: sentence 2: 'causal' is not in the English sentence

en.text: The hippocampus is a key structure found in the brains of people and numerous other vertebrate species, sitting in the archicortex within both brain hemispheres.

In humans, this region works alongside the dentate gyrus and subiculum to form the hippocampal formation within the limbic system, helping transfer short-term memories into long-term storage and supporting spatial memory needed for navigating the environment.
The region sends direct neural signals to the neocortex and receives indirect signals back from it, a site where long-term potentiation, a type of neural plasticity, was first identified.

facts.statement: This structure exists as a pair of nuclear complexes found in the cerebral hemispheres of all vertebrates.
The amygdala is classified as a component of the limbic system.
In primate brains, this region sits on the inner side of the temporal lobes.
The structure is composed of numerous nuclei, which are themselves divided into smaller subnuclei.
The most frequent division of the amygdala includes basolateral, central, cortical, and medial nuclei along with intercalated cell clusters.
This brain area is primarily responsible for handling memory, making decisions, and generating emotional reactions such as fear, anxiety, and aggression.
Karl Friedrich Burdach was the first person to identify and give a name to this structure in the year 1822.

en.text: The amygdala exists as a pair of nuclear complexes within the limbic system, located on the inner side of the temporal lobes in primate brains.

This structure consists of numerous nuclei divided into smaller subnuclei, with the most frequent division including basolateral, central, cortical, and medial nuclei along with intercalated cell clusters.
It is primarily responsible for handling memory, making decisions, and generating emotional reactions such as fear, anxiety, and aggression.

es.text: La amígdala existe como un par de complejos nucleares dentro del sistema límbico, situada en la cara medial de los lóbulos temporales en el cerebro de los primates.

Esta estructura está compuesta por numerosos núcleos divididos en subnúcleos más pequeños, siendo la división más frecuente la que incluye los núcleos basolateral, central, cortical y medial, junto con cúmulos de células intercaladas.
Su función principal consiste en procesar la memoria, tomar decisiones y generar reacciones emocionales como el miedo, la ansiedad y la agresión.

facts.statement: Known by its Latin name meaning 'little brain', this structure is a key component of the hindbrain found in every vertebrate species.
In humans, the organ is positioned at the base of the brain, situated directly beneath the cerebral hemispheres.
The surface features distinct parallel grooves that hide a thin, continuous sheet of tissue folded densely like an accordion.
The tissue contains a highly organized arrangement of neurons, with Purkinje cells and granule cells being the most significant types.
Signals generated in the outer cortex are transmitted through small deep nuclei located within the white matter core of the structure.
The region contributes to motor control, cognitive tasks like attention and language, and the regulation of emotional responses including fear and pleasure.
While it does not start voluntary movements, the structure is essential for coordinating motion, ensuring precision, and maintaining accurate timing.
The organ processes signals from spinal cord sensory systems and other brain areas to adjust and refine motor actions.
Injury to this area results in problems with fine motor skills, balance, posture, and the ability to learn new movements.
Beyond immediate movement control, the structure is required for various forms of motor learning, particularly those involving sensorimotor connections.

en.text: Known as the 'little brain,' the cerebellum is a hindbrain component located at the base of the human brain, directly beneath the cerebral hemispheres.
Its surface displays parallel grooves that conceal a densely folded sheet of tissue containing organized neurons, including Purkinje and granule cells.
While it does not initiate voluntary movements, this region coordinates motion, ensures precision, and regulates cognitive tasks and emotional responses.

es.text: Conocido como el «cerebrito», el cerebelo es una estructura del encéfalo posterior situada en la base del cerebro humano, justo debajo de los hemisferios cerebrales.
Su superficie presenta surcos paralelos que ocultan una lámina de tejido densamente plegada, repleta de neuronas organizadas, entre ellas las células de Purkinje y las células granulosas.
Aunque no inicia los movimientos voluntarios, esta región coordina el movimiento, garantiza la precisión y regula las tareas cognitivas y las respuestas emocionales.

facts.statement: The brainstem is the stalk-like structure at the back of the brain that links the cerebrum to the spinal cord.
The midbrain connects to the thalamus through the tentorial notch, and the diencephalon is sometimes considered part of the brainstem.
The brainstem is very small, accounting for only about 2.6 percent of the brain's total weight.
It plays a critical role in regulating heart and respiratory functions, including heart rate and breathing rate.
The brainstem supplies the main motor and sensory nerves to the face and neck through the cranial nerves.
Ten pairs of cranial nerves originate from the brainstem.
The brainstem carries motor and sensory pathways between the rest of the brain and the body, including the corticospinal tract, dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway, and spinothalamic tract.

en.text: The brainstem is a small, stalk-like structure at the back of the brain that links the cerebrum to the spinal cord, accounting for about 2.6 percent of the brain's total weight.
It regulates vital functions such as heart rate and breathing, while supplying ten pairs of cranial nerves that provide motor and sensory connections to the face and neck.

Additionally, the brainstem carries major motor and sensory pathways, including the corticospinal tract, dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway, and spinothalamic tract, between the rest of the brain and the body.

es.text: El tronco encefálico es una estructura pequeña y de forma de tallo, situada en la parte posterior del cerebro, que conecta el encéfalo con la médula espinal y representa aproximadamente el 2,6 % del peso total del cerebro.
Regula funciones vitales como la frecuencia cardíaca y la respiración, y da origen a diez pares de nervios craneales que proporcionan conexiones motoras y sensoriales a la cara y el cuello.

Además, el tronco encefálico transporta las principales vías motoras y sensoriales, como el tracto piramidal, la vía espinotalámica y el lemnisco medial de la columna dorsal, entre el resto del cerebro y el cuerpo.

facts.statement: The striatum is a group of connected nuclei that forms the biggest part of the subcortical basal ganglia.
It plays a key role in motor control and reward processing, receiving glutamate and dopamine signals while acting as the main entry point for the rest of the basal ganglia.
The structure is responsible for coordinating cognitive tasks such as planning actions, making decisions, feeling motivated, and perceiving rewards.
In primates, the region is split into ventral and dorsal sections based on their specific functions and neural connections.
The dorsal striatum contains the caudate nucleus and the putamen.
A white matter tract called the internal capsule runs through the dorsal striatum to separate the caudate nucleus from the putamen.
The name striatum refers to the striped visual pattern created by the alternating grey and white matter.

en.text: The striatum is a group of connected nuclei that forms the largest part of the subcortical basal ganglia, and in primates it splits into ventral and dorsal sections.
The dorsal section contains the caudate nucleus and the putamen, which a white matter tract called the internal capsule separates.

Acting as the main entry point for the basal ganglia, this structure processes glutamate and dopamine signals to coordinate motor control, reward perception, and cognitive tasks like planning and decision-making.

es.text: El estriado es un conjunto de núcleos interconectados que constituye la mayor parte de los ganglios basales subcorticales y, en los primates, se divide en secciones ventral y dorsal.
La sección dorsal alberga el núcleo caudado y el putamen, dos estructuras que separa un haz de sustancia blanca conocido como cápsula interna.

Al actuar como el principal punto de entrada de los ganglios basales, esta estructura procesa las señales de glutamato y dopamina para coordinar el control motor, la percepción de la recompensa y tareas cognitivas como la planificación y la toma de decisiones.

facts.statement: The globus pallidus is a key structure within the brain's subcortical basal ganglia, also referred to as the paleostriatum or dorsal pallidum.
This region is divided into two neighboring sections: an external (lateral) segment and an internal (medial) segment.
Although located in the telencephalon, the globus pallidus works closely with the diencephalic subthalamus as part of the extrapyramidal motor system.
The primary neural inputs to this area come from the striatum, while its main direct outputs go to the thalamus and substantia nigra.
The globus pallidus does not receive direct connections from the cerebral cortex but does get significant input from the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus.
The name globus pallidus is derived from Latin words meaning "pale globe".

en.text: The globus pallidus, a key structure within the brain's subcortical basal ganglia, is divided into two neighboring sections: an external (lateral) segment and an internal (medial) segment.

Although located in the telencephalon, this region works closely with the diencephalic subthalamus as part of the extrapyramidal motor system, receiving primary neural inputs from the striatum while sending main direct outputs to the thalamus and substantia nigra.
It does not receive direct connections from the cerebral cortex but does get significant input from the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus.

es.text: El globo pálido, una estructura clave de los ganglios basales subcorticales del cerebro, se divide en dos secciones vecinas: un segmento externo (lateral) y un segmento interno (medial).

Aunque se sitúa en el telencéfalo, esta región colabora estrechamente con el subtálamo del diencéfalo como parte del sistema motor extrapiramidal, ya que recibe las entradas neuronales principales del estriado y envía sus salidas directas principales al tálamo y a la sustancia negra.
No recibe conexiones directas de la corteza cerebral, pero sí obtiene una entrada significativa de los núcleos intralaminares del tálamo.

facts.statement: The ventricular system consists of four connected spaces called cerebral ventricles located in the brain.
Each ventricle contains choroid plexus tissue that generates the circulating cerebrospinal fluid.
The system links to the spinal cord's central canal starting at the fourth ventricle, enabling cerebrospinal fluid to move.
The inner surfaces of the ventricles and the spinal cord's central canal are covered by ependyma, a specialized epithelial tissue.
Tight junctions between ependymal cells form the blood–cerebrospinal fluid barrier.

en.text: The ventricular system comprises four connected cerebral ventricles within the brain, each housing choroid plexus tissue that generates circulating cerebrospinal fluid.
Beginning at the fourth ventricle, this network links to the spinal cord's central canal, while ependyma, a specialized epithelial tissue, lines the inner surfaces of both structures.
Tight junctions between these ependymal cells establish the blood–cerebrospinal fluid barrier.

es.text: El sistema ventricular está formado por cuatro ventrículos cerebrales interconectados, cada uno de los cuales alberga tejido del plexo coroideo que produce el líquido cefalorraquídeo en circulación.

A partir del cuarto ventrículo, esta red se conecta con el canal central de la médula espinal, mientras que el epéndimo, un tejido epitelial especializado, reviste las superficies internas de ambas estructuras.
Las uniones estrechas entre estas células ependimarias establecen la barrera sangre-líquido cefalorraquídeo.

facts.statement: The optic chiasm is the specific area within the brain where the optic nerves intersect.
This structure sits at the base of the brain, directly beneath the hypothalamus.
The name derives from Greek words meaning 'crossing' or 'to mark with an X'.
All vertebrate species possess an optic chiasm.
In lampreys and hagfishes, the chiasm is situated inside the brain rather than at its base.
A nerve crossing that occurs along the midline within the brain is technically referred to as a decussation.

en.text: The optic chiasm, the specific area where the optic nerves intersect, sits at the base of the brain directly beneath the hypothalamus.
All vertebrate species possess this structure, although in lampreys and hagfishes it is situated inside the brain rather than at its base.

facts.statement: The name of this brain region derives from Greek words meaning 'under' and 'chamber'.
This structure sits beneath the thalamus and belongs to the limbic system.
It constitutes the base of the diencephalon.
In people, the hypothalamus is roughly the size of an almond.
A key role of this area is connecting the nervous and endocrine systems through the pituitary gland.
It manages specific metabolic processes and various activities of the autonomic nervous system.
The region produces and releases neurohormones that either trigger or block hormone release from the pituitary gland.
It regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst, fatigue, sleep, and circadian rhythms, while also influencing parenting, maternal attachment, and social behaviors like aggression and sexuality.

en.text: Named from Greek words meaning 'under' and 'chamber', the hypothalamus sits beneath the thalamus as part of the limbic system and forms the base of the diencephalon.
In people, this almond-sized structure connects the nervous and endocrine systems through the pituitary gland.
It manages specific metabolic processes and autonomic nervous system activities by producing neurohormones that trigger or block hormone release from the pituitary gland.

Furthermore, the region regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst, fatigue, sleep, and circadian rhythms, while influencing parenting, maternal attachment, and social behaviors like aggression and sexuality.

es.text: Su nombre proviene de palabras griegas que significan «debajo» y «cámara», y el hipotálamo se sitúa bajo el tálamo como parte del sistema límbico, formando la base del diencéfalo.
En los seres humanos, esta estructura del tamaño de una almendra conecta los sistemas nervioso y endocrino a través de la glándula pituitaria.

Gestiona procesos metabólicos específicos y actividades del sistema nervioso autónomo mediante la producción de neurohormonas que activan o bloquean la liberación de hormonas desde la glándula pituitaria.

Además, esta región regula la temperatura corporal, el hambre, la sed, la fatiga, el sueño y los ritmos circadianos, al tiempo que influye en la crianza, el apego materno y comportamientos sociales como la agresividad y la sexualidad.

facts.statement: The epithalamus is a dorsal section of the diencephalon located toward the back of the brain.
The pineal gland is one of the structures contained within the epithalamus.
The habenular nuclei are part of the epithalamus.
The stria medullaris is a component of the epithalamus.
The anterior and posterior paraventricular nuclei are located within the epithalamus.
The posterior commissure is included in the epithalamus.

en.text: The epithalamus is a dorsal section of the diencephalon located toward the back of the brain.
This region contains the pineal gland, habenular nuclei, stria medullaris, anterior and posterior paraventricular nuclei, and the posterior commissure.

es.text: El epitalamo es una sección dorsal del diencéfalo situada hacia la parte posterior del cerebro.
Esta región alberga la glándula pineal, los núcleos habenulares, la estría medular, los núcleos paraventriculares anterior y posterior, y la comisura posterior.

facts.statement: This tissue is located within the central nervous system and consists primarily of myelinated axons, which are also referred to as tracts.
It plays an active role in learning and overall brain function by regulating how action potentials are distributed, serving as a relay, and coordinating signals between various brain areas.
The region gets its name from its pale look, which is caused by the high lipid content found in myelin.
In laboratory specimens, the tissue appears white because it is typically preserved using formaldehyde.
Without formaldehyde preservation, the tissue looks pinkish-white to the unaided eye, a result of myelin being mostly lipid tissue interspersed with capillaries.

en.text: Located within the central nervous system, white matter consists primarily of myelinated axons, also known as tracts, which give the tissue its pale appearance due to high lipid content.
This structure actively supports learning and overall brain function by regulating action potential distribution, serving as a relay, and coordinating signals between various brain areas.

es.text: Ubicada en el sistema nervioso central, la sustancia blanca está compuesta principalmente por axones mielinizados, también conocidos como tractos, que le confieren su aspecto pálido debido a su alto contenido lipídico.

Esta estructura apoya activamente el aprendizaje y la función cerebral general al regular la distribución del potencial de acción, actuar como relé y coordinar las señales entre distintas áreas del cerebro.
